primitives.name: Observation Model Constraint
primitives.verbatim_quote: ## Guard 1: the observation model must be binomial, not Gaussian Contract claim under test: the module header declares X is a **binomial** matrix, a proportion over a known denominator (completions/targets, EPA>0 plays/snaps).
primitives.assumptions: Observations follow binomial distribution with known denominator; empirical Bayes or logit-normal required for valid inference.
primitives.breakdown_regime: When fitted using Gaussian ALS, produces out-of-support values such as negative probabilities.

layer2.mapping: GLMF binomial constraint maps to Bayesian posterior mean estimation with conjugate priors; Gaussian fit violates probabilistic consistency.

primitives.name: Probability Range Enforcement
primitives.verbatim_quote: Fitted cells must stay inside the probability range Asserts: after fitting, `glmfPredict` returns a value in `[0, 1]` for every `(u, i)` cell.
primitives.assumptions: Model outputs must remain within valid probability space; no unconstrained linear combinations allowed.
primitives.breakdown_regime: Negative or >1 predictions indicate violation of range constraint.

layer2.mapping: Enforces kernel-level projection onto valid probability simplex; prevents numerical instability in downstream inference.
layer2.telemetry: Out-of-range prediction detection via assertion checks.

reasoning_traces.think:
The core issue lies in applying Gaussian alternating least squares (ALS) to binomial data—specifically, ratio values derived from counts. This misalignment causes the model to generate predictions outside [0,1], violating fundamental probability axioms. The first primitive enforces that the observation model must be binomial, requiring either beta-binomial empirical Bayes or logit-normal transformation. The second primitive ensures all predictions lie within [0,1], failing when negative or exceeding-one values appear. The third primitive highlights that trial counts affect predictive precision; ignoring them leads to identical predictions regardless of data reliability. These failures reveal a systemic mismatch between statistical modeling assumptions and implementation details, where the current codebase uses inappropriate regression techniques for inherently bounded data types.
